bullets: Blake was a **Christian who attacked the organised Church**: he believed it taught people to repress natural feelings, which then turned poisonous.
The poem was originally drafted under the title **Christian Forbearance**: the ironic point is that ‘forbearing’ (not expressing) anger can be more dangerous than expressing it.
The **Garden of Eden** story (Genesis 3) runs underneath: a garden, a tree, an apple, a forbidden act, death. Blake rewrites it so the human speaker, not the serpent, sets the trap.
Written in the 1790s, during the French Revolution, when Blake saw how repression bred violence. You can link this cautiously: suppressed resentment explodes.

callouts.p: Do not just say ‘Blake was religious’. Say how the Genesis allusion changes the meaning: the speaker becomes the tempter, so Blake suggests evil starts in ordinary human feelings, not in an outside devil.

core.h: Context (AO3): Blake, Songs of Experience and religion
core.p: William Blake (1757–1827) was a Romantic poet, painter and engraver who printed his own illustrated books. A Poison Tree was published in **Songs of Experience (1794)**, the companion to Songs of Innocence (1789). The ‘Experience’ poems show the world after innocence is lost: corrupted by institutions, repression and sin.

bullets: **Conflict type**: personal, psychological and moral conflict between two people; also inner conflict that the speaker refuses to resolve.
**Big message**: communication prevents conflict; repression and pride turn feelings into violence.
**Perspective**: first-person confession with no apology, which lets the reader judge the speaker.
core.p: The poem is an **allegory** of anger. The speaker contrasts telling a friend about anger (it ends) with hiding anger from an enemy (it grows). He then nurtures the anger with fear, tears, false smiles and deception, until it bears an apple. The enemy, tempted, steals into the garden at night and is found dead under the tree in the morning. The speaker is glad.

bullets: The simple sing-song form **contrasts** with the murderous content: the gap between form and meaning creates a sinister, ironic tone.
Stanza 1 works like a **thesis**; stanzas 2–3 show the anger growing; stanza 4 shows the result. It is a cause-and-effect narrative, like a parable.
**Anaphora** of ‘And’ (nine lines start with it) builds momentum: the growth feels unstoppable.
The **tense shift** to the present in the last couplet (‘I see’) makes the ending immediate.
The last line is the only one where the result is shown rather than stated: the poem stops at the image of the body, leaving judgement to the reader.
core.p: Four quatrains of **rhyming couplets** in a mostly **trochaic tetrameter** rhythm (stressed–unstressed beats, seven or eight syllables a line). The form is deliberately simple, like a hymn or a children’s rhyme.

bullets: Conflict **grows from small, private feelings**: the poem traces a murder back to a moment of silence.
Conflict is **cultivated deliberately**: the gardening verbs make the speaker responsible.
Conflict **corrupts both sides**: the foe’s envy and theft make him complicit.
Conflict is shown as **sin**: wrath, deception and theft echo the Fall of Man.
The **absence of guilt** is the most disturbing feature; compare Hardy’s soldier who is troubled by his act.

callouts.p: Hidden anger, deliberately nurtured, becomes deadly revenge, and the speaker is glad.

Endings: Blake’s gladness vs Rossetti’s son as a weapon
essays.q: Compare how hidden feelings lead to conflict in A Poison Tree and Cousin Kate.
essays.text:
Blake presents conflict as something that grows from a private decision. In the first stanza the balanced lines set ‘friend’ against ‘foe’, and the speaker’s choice, ‘I told it not’, makes the anger ‘grow’. The verb begins an extended metaphor in which he ‘watered’ and ‘sunned’ the anger like a gardener, so the reader sees that the hatred is cultivated deliberately, morning and night. Rossetti’s speaker, by contrast, does not choose silence; it is imposed on her. As a Victorian ‘fallen woman’ she is called an ‘outcast thing’ by the neighbours, and the dehumanising noun shows how society, rather than she herself, has hidden her worth.

Both poets use natural imagery to show innocence corrupted. Blake’s tree bears an ‘apple bright’, an allusion to Genesis that turns the speaker into the tempter; since Blake attacked a Church that taught people to repress feeling, the poem suggests that this repression creates sin. Rossetti also uses religious and natural images: her speaker ‘might have been a dove’, a symbol of purity and peace, but instead sits and ‘howl[s] in dust’. Yet where Blake’s ending is chillingly calm, with the foe ‘outstretched’ and the speaker ‘glad’, Rossetti’s is defiant: her son is ‘my shame, my pride’, and the antithesis shows that she has turned society’s judgement into a weapon against the lord who has no heir. In both poems hidden feelings become a form of revenge, but Blake warns against it while Rossetti invites sympathy for it.
essays.thesis: Both poets show that feelings which cannot be spoken turn into revenge, but Blake’s speaker chooses silence and is corrupted by it, while Rossetti’s speaker is silenced by society and turns her pain into defiance.
why: Comparative from the first sentence: ‘by contrast’, ‘both’, ‘yet where’.
AO2 precision: verbs, extended metaphor, allusion, antithesis, endings.
AO3 woven in: Blake and the Church; the Victorian ‘fallen woman’.
Evaluative final sentence answers the question directly.

mistakes.w: The poem is about a real murder Blake committed.

mistakes.w: The speaker learns his lesson at the end.

poem.how: Read the stanza on the left, then each numbered note on the right. Colours tell you which AO the note is for.

stanzas.label: Stanza 1
lines: I was angry with my friend;
I told my wrath, my wrath did end.
I was angry with my foe:
I told it not, my wrath did grow.

notes.n: Blunt first-person **confession**. The monosyllables and the simple subject–verb–object syntax make it sound like a nursery rhyme or a moral lesson, which is exactly what it turns out to be.
notes.w: I was angry with my friend;

notes.n: Speaking honestly ends anger. The **repetition** of ‘my wrath’ either side of the caesura makes the anger appear and vanish in one line.
notes.w: I told my wrath, my wrath did end.

notes.n: **Antithesis** with ‘friend’. The whole stanza is two balanced couplets: lines 1–2 show the healthy choice, lines 3–4 the dangerous one. Structure = moral choice.
The key idea of the poem: **suppressed anger grows**. ‘Grow’ is the first hint of the extended metaphor of a plant that will dominate the rest of the poem.
notes.w: I told it not, my wrath did grow.

notes.n: ‘Wrath’ is biblical (one of the seven deadly sins), so the poem is about sin, not just irritation. Blake was a deeply religious but anti-establishment Christian.

stanzas.label: Stanza 2
lines: And I watered it in fears,
Night and morning with my tears:
And I sunned it with smiles,

notes.n: **Extended metaphor**: anger is a plant he tends. ‘Watered’ and ‘sunned’ are gardening verbs: he actively cultivates the hatred, so the conflict is deliberate.
notes.w: And I watered it in fears,

notes.n: Time phrase shows obsession: the anger is fed constantly. The relentless ‘And… And… And’ (**polysyndeton/anaphora**) shows how the feeling keeps accumulating.
Ironically the speaker suffers too: hidden anger feeds on his own misery. Conflict damages the person who holds it.
**Sibilance** (soft, deceitful) creates a sly, hissing sound linked to the serpent in Eden. He smiles at his foe while plotting: appearance versus reality.

stanzas.label: Stanza 3
lines: And it grew both day and night.
Till it bore an apple bright.
And my foe beheld it shine,
And he knew that it was mine.

notes.n: **Biblical allusion** to the forbidden fruit in Genesis: temptation that leads to death. The anger has now produced something attractive but deadly.
The fruit ‘shines’ to attract the foe. Revenge is made to look beautiful, which is part of its danger.
The foe is tempted by envy: he wants what belongs to the speaker. Blake shows that both men are corrupted, not just the speaker.
Possession and pride. The **rhyming couplets** (night/bright, shine/mine) stay regular and childlike, which makes the sinister content more chilling.
notes.w: And he knew that it was mine.

stanzas.label: Stanza 4
lines: When the night had veiled the pole;
In the morning glad I see;
My foe outstretched beneath the tree.

notes.n: The foe sins too (stealing), echoing Adam and Eve. Conflict here is mutual: neither is innocent.
Darkness ‘veils’ the pole star: secrecy and moral blindness. The crime happens hidden, just as the anger was hidden.
notes.w: When the night had veiled the pole;

notes.n: The shocking word is **‘glad’**. The speaker feels no guilt. The switch to the **present tense** makes the moment immediate and unsettling, as if we are watching with him.
notes.w: In the morning glad I see;

notes.n: **Ambiguous ending**: the foe is dead (or at least poisoned). The tree, a symbol of life, has become a symbol of death. Compare the speaker’s lack of remorse with the guilt in The Man He Killed.
notes.w: My foe outstretched beneath the tree.

summary: A Poison Tree (1794) is a four-stanza allegory in which anger that is hidden and nursed grows like a plant until it bears a poisoned fruit that kills the speaker’s enemy; Edexcel wants you to compare how it presents conflict, revenge and the danger of suppressed feelings, with context from Blake’s Romantic and religious thinking.

terms.d: A story in which characters and events stand for moral or abstract ideas; here the tree stands for anger.
A metaphor developed across several lines or the whole poem (anger as a growing plant).
Four stressed–unstressed beats per line; gives a chanting, nursery-rhyme rhythm.
Repeating a word at the start of successive lines (‘And…’).
A reference to the Bible that adds layers of meaning (the apple, the garden).
Placing opposite ideas side by side in balanced phrases (friend/foe, end/grow).
